skills.title: Tiny Start
skills.use_when: Task initiation is blocked by overwhelm, perfectionism, low energy, or unclear first steps.
steps: Name the task in one sentence.
Shrink it until the first action takes about two minutes or less.
Place only the needed item or screen in front of the person.
Start a short timer and stop or continue by choice when it ends.
adaptations: Offer a one-word choice between two starts.
Use voice notes instead of typing when helpful.

skills.title: Working Memory Externalization
skills.use_when: The person keeps losing steps, ideas, or intentions.
steps: Capture the thought immediately outside the brain.
Keep one visible list for the current task.
Cross off or hide completed steps.
Move future ideas to a parking-lot list.
avoid: Do not rely on 'just remember'.

skills.title: Transition Bridge
skills.use_when: Stopping one activity and beginning another is hard.
steps: Name the current activity and the next activity.
Give a predictable warning.
Choose one bridge action such as save, bathroom, drink, stretch, or pack materials.
Use the same cue to begin the next activity.
adaptations: Use visual countdowns or alarms if they help; avoid them if they increase distress.

skills.title: Body Double
skills.use_when: Presence helps task initiation or persistence.
steps: Agree on the task and duration.
The support person stays present without taking over.
Use brief check-ins rather than constant reminders.
End with a neutral recap, not a performance judgment.

skills.title: Time Map
skills.use_when: Time blindness makes planning unreliable.
steps: Estimate the task in chunks.
Add setup, transition, and recovery time.
Anchor to a real event or alarm.
Review actual time afterward without shame and update the estimate.

skills.title: Sensory Map
skills.use_when: Overload, shutdown, irritability, pain, or fatigue may be affected by sensory input.
steps: Check sound, light, touch, temperature, smell, movement, hunger, thirst, pain, and social load.
Identify one input to reduce and one regulating input to add.
Lower communication demand while regulating.
Reassess after a quiet interval.
avoid: Do not force eye contact or verbal explanation during overload.

skills.title: Shutdown Support
skills.use_when: Speech, movement, decision-making, or processing has dropped sharply under stress.
steps: Reduce demands and questions.
Offer yes/no, pointing, typing, AAC, or silence.
Reduce sensory load and preserve physical safety.
Delay nonessential problem solving until processing returns.
avoid: Do not interpret reduced speech as defiance.

skills.title: Meltdown Recovery
skills.use_when: The nervous system is overloaded and behavioral control is reduced.
steps: Prioritize safety and lower stimulation.
Reduce audience and demands.
Allow safe regulating movement or stillness.
After recovery, review triggers and supports without blame.
avoid: Do not use punishment, argument, or forced processing during peak overload.

skills.title: Burnout Load Reduction
skills.use_when: Sustained overload, masking, demands, or insufficient recovery have reduced capacity.
steps: List essential and deferrable demands.
Protect recovery time and sensory safety.
Use communication shortcuts and accessibility supports.
Rebuild activity gradually based on capacity rather than guilt.
avoid: Do not frame reduced capacity as laziness.

skills.title: Predictable Transition
skills.use_when: Change or uncertainty is increasing distress.
steps: Describe what will happen, in what order, and what is uncertain.
Name a fallback plan.
Allow a regulating object, routine, or communication method.
Give a clear ending cue and recovery option.

skills.title: Thought Record
skills.use_when: A strong emotion is linked to a specific interpretation or prediction.
steps: Describe the situation briefly.
Name the automatic thought.
Rate emotion intensity.
List evidence supporting and not supporting the thought.
Write a more balanced thought that fits the evidence.
Choose one helpful action.
avoid: Do not use cognitive restructuring to argue someone out of a real safety concern or discrimination experience.

skills.title: Behavioral Activation
skills.use_when: Low mood or avoidance has reduced meaningful activity.
steps: Choose one very small activity tied to care, mastery, connection, or pleasure.
Set a low-effort version.
Schedule a specific start cue.
Record mood before and after without demanding improvement.
avoid: Do not prescribe exertion that conflicts with medical or disability limits.

skills.title: Structured Problem Solving
skills.use_when: A solvable problem is looping without a concrete plan.
steps: Define the problem narrowly.
Brainstorm options without judging them.
Compare effort, safety, accessibility, and likely benefit.
Pick one testable step.
Review the result and revise.

skills.title: Worry Window
skills.use_when: Repetitive worry is consuming the day.
steps: Capture the worry in a note.
Choose a short scheduled time to review worries.
During the day, redirect to the present task when possible.
At the scheduled time, separate actionable problems from uncertainty.
avoid: Do not postpone urgent safety or medical concerns.

skills.title: Graded Practice
skills.use_when: Avoidance is maintaining fear and the target is safe, consensual, and appropriate for gradual practice.
steps: Define the feared but safe activity.
Create small steps from easier to harder.
Choose a manageable step and coping support.
Repeat by consent and update the hierarchy from experience.
avoid: Do not use for trauma processing, medical risk, abuse situations, psychosis content, self-harm urges, or unsafe environments without qualified clinical guidance.

skills.title: STOP
skills.use_when: A strong urge may lead to an impulsive action.
steps: Stop.
Take a step back physically or mentally.
Observe body sensations, emotions, thoughts, urges, and facts.
Proceed mindfully toward the next effective action.

skills.title: TIPP
skills.use_when: High physiological arousal needs short-term downshifting.
steps: Use a safe temperature change that does not conflict with medical needs.
Use brief movement only within physical capacity.
Slow the exhale and pace breathing comfortably.
Try paired muscle tension and release if safe and comfortable.
avoid: Do not use intense exercise or extreme temperature when medically unsafe; use gentler grounding instead.

skills.title: ACCEPTS
skills.use_when: Short-term distraction is needed to survive a distress spike without making things worse.
steps: Choose a safe activity, contribution, comparison, emotion shift, temporary pushing-away, different thoughts, or sensory focus.
Use it as a temporary bridge.
Return to the problem later if action is needed.

skills.title: Check the Facts
skills.use_when: Emotion intensity may be amplified by assumptions or incomplete information.
steps: Name the prompting event.
Separate observations from interpretations.
Check assumptions against available evidence.
Ask whether the emotion and intensity fit the facts.
Choose problem solving, acceptance, or an emotion-regulation skill.
avoid: Do not dismiss lived experience or real danger as a thinking error.

skills.title: Opposite Action
skills.use_when: An emotion or urge does not fit the facts or acting on it would be ineffective.
steps: Name the emotion and urge.
Check the facts and safety.
Identify the effective opposite behavior.
Do the opposite action fully enough to test its effect.
avoid: Do not use opposite action to override legitimate boundaries, pain limits, medical symptoms, or danger signals.

skills.title: DEAR MAN
skills.use_when: A clear request, refusal, or boundary is needed.
steps: Describe the facts briefly.
Express feelings or impact.
Assert the request or boundary clearly.
Reinforce why cooperation helps.
Stay mindful of the goal.
Appear confident in a way that fits the person.
Negotiate where appropriate without abandoning essential safety or consent.

skills.title: GIVE
skills.use_when: The relationship matters during a conversation.
steps: Be gentle.
Show interest.
Validate what makes sense in the other person's experience.
Use an easy manner that fits the situation.

skills.title: FAST
skills.use_when: Self-respect needs protection in an interpersonal situation.
steps: Be fair to self and others.
Avoid unnecessary apologies for existing or having needs.
Stick to values.
Be truthful.

skills.title: Behavior Chain Analysis
skills.use_when: A behavior needs a no-blame map of what led to it and what could change next time.
steps: Name the target behavior neutrally.
Identify vulnerabilities before the event.
Map prompting event, thoughts, body sensations, emotions, actions, and consequences.
Find missing skills or support points.
Choose one prevention step and one repair step.
avoid: Do not turn chain analysis into interrogation, punishment, or proof of moral failure.

skills.title: Structured Psychiatric Check-In
skills.use_when: The person wants to summarize symptoms and functioning for themselves or a clinician.
steps: Review mood, anxiety, irritability, energy, sleep, appetite, concentration, trauma symptoms, dissociation, unusual perceptions/thoughts, substance use, and safety.
Record onset, frequency, intensity, duration, triggers, and functional impact.
Note medication taken as prescribed, missed doses, and side effects without changing treatment.
Identify what changed since the last check-in and what needs professional follow-up.
avoid: Do not convert a checklist score into a diagnosis.

skills.title: Clinician Visit Preparation
skills.use_when: A visit is coming up and important information needs organization.
steps: List the top three concerns.
Add timeline, examples, and functional impact.
List current medications and side effects exactly as taken/reported.
Write questions and desired outcomes.
Include safety concerns and major recent changes first.

skills.title: Medication Journal
skills.use_when: The person wants to track medication experience without changing treatment.
steps: Record medication name exactly as prescribed, time taken, missed dose if any, perceived benefit, side effects, sleep, appetite, and relevant symptoms.
Mark urgent reactions for professional or emergency review.
Bring trends to the prescriber or pharmacist.
avoid: Do not advise dose changes, taper schedules, substitutions, or combining substances.

skills.title: Reality-Grounded Support
skills.use_when: A person reports paranoia, hallucinations, or unusual beliefs.
steps: Acknowledge fear or distress.
Avoid confirming the unusual belief as fact.
Focus on what is directly observable and immediate safety.
Encourage contact with a trusted person or clinician when symptoms are new, worsening, or impairing functioning.
avoid: Do not investigate, elaborate, or role-play the delusional framework as true.

skills.title: 5-4-3-2-1 Grounding
skills.use_when: The person feels flooded, panicky, detached, or stuck in looping thoughts and sensory grounding is tolerable.
steps: Notice five things you can see.
Notice four things you can feel safely.
Notice three things you can hear.
Notice two things you can smell or imagine smelling.
Notice one thing you can taste or one slow breath.
adaptations: Use fewer senses if sensory input is overwhelming.
Use one object, texture, sound, or fact if counting is too much.

skills.title: Dissociation Anchor
skills.use_when: The person feels unreal, detached, foggy, or disconnected.
steps: State the current date and location if known.
Name one reliable fact about the present moment.
Press feet, hands, or another supported body area into a stable surface if comfortable.
Use a familiar sensory anchor.
Reduce demands until orientation improves.
avoid: Do not force intense sensory stimulation.

skills.title: Grief Support
skills.use_when: Loss is producing waves of sadness, numbness, anger, longing, or disorientation.
steps: Name what hurts most right now.
Choose care for the next hour rather than solving grief.
Use memory, ritual, connection, rest, food, hydration, or practical support as wanted.
Expect grief intensity to vary rather than follow a fixed timeline.

skills.title: Sleep Wind-Down
skills.use_when: The person wants a low-pressure sleep routine.
steps: Choose a repeatable wind-down cue.
Reduce stimulating tasks when possible.
Prepare accessibility, medications as prescribed, hydration, bathroom, temperature, and sensory needs before settling.
If sleep does not come, use a quiet low-demand activity instead of escalating self-criticism.
avoid: Do not present sleep hygiene as a cure for psychiatric or medical sleep disorders.

skills.title: Symptom Journal
skills.use_when: Symptoms need organized tracking for self-management or a clinician.
steps: Record symptom, start time, intensity, duration, location, triggers, associated symptoms, function impact, and what helped or worsened it.
Add relevant device readings only if already part of the person's care plan.
Mark new severe or rapidly worsening symptoms for prompt professional review.
avoid: Do not use the journal to delay emergency care.

skills.title: Accessibility-Aware Care Plan
skills.use_when: A care task conflicts with mobility, pain, fatigue, sensory, communication, or caregiver limits.
steps: Define the goal rather than one required method.
Identify access barriers.
Create seated, bed-based, AAC, low-energy, or assisted alternatives where appropriate.
Choose the safest workable version and document needed accommodations.

skills.title: Follow Existing Medical Plan
skills.use_when: A health condition already has clinician instructions.
steps: Use the written plan as the source of truth for thresholds, medication, devices, and escalation.
Record what happened and what action the plan directs.
Contact the relevant clinician/pharmacist when instructions are unclear or symptoms are changing.
avoid: Do not invent personalized thresholds, correction doses, missed-dose instructions, or device settings.

skills.title: Medical Emergency Escalation
skills.use_when: Clear emergency symptoms may be present.
steps: Stop chatbot problem solving.
Contact local emergency services now.
Get a nearby person if possible.
Follow the person's existing emergency plan while help is coming.
avoid: Do not reassure away severe symptoms or delay emergency help for a worksheet.
